module_title: CSR, Oppression & Mismanagement, and the Rule in Foss v. Harbottle
introduction: Tailored for advanced legal exams and UPSC Law Optional, this level explores the revolutionary corporate social responsibility mandates of the 2013 Act, the protection of minority shareholders, and the sweeping powers of the NCLT.

core_concepts.title: Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR - Section 135)
core_concepts.description:
India is the first country to legally mandate CSR.
- Applicability: Applies to any company (in the immediately preceding financial year) having: (1) Net worth of ₹500 Cr or more, OR (2) Turnover of ₹1000 Cr or more, OR (3) Net Profit of ₹5 Cr or more.
- The Mandate: The company MUST spend at least **2% of its average net profits** made during the 3 immediately preceding financial years on CSR activities (e.g., education, poverty eradication, environmental sustainability).
- Compliance: Failure to spend requires the unspent amount to be transferred to a specific government fund (like the PM CARES Fund) within 6 months.

core_concepts.title: The Rule in Foss v. Harbottle (Majority Rule)
core_concepts.description:
A fundamental common law principle regarding internal corporate disputes.
- The Rule (1843): The court will not interfere in the internal management of a company. If a wrong is done to the company, the *company itself* is the proper plaintiff to sue, not individual shareholders. Since the majority rules the company, the minority cannot usually sue on behalf of the company.

core_concepts.title: Protection of Minority: Oppression and Mismanagement (Sec 241-244)
core_concepts.description:
The statutory exception to *Foss v. Harbottle*.
- Oppression: Conduct that is harsh, burdensome, and wrongful towards the minority shareholders (e.g., majority shareholders systematically depriving minority of dividends).
- Mismanagement: Managing affairs in a manner prejudicial to the interests of the company (e.g., siphoning off funds).
- Remedy: Under the 2013 Act, eligible members (at least 100 members or 10% of total members) can directly approach the **National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT)**. The NCLT has draconian powers, including removing directors, restricting share transfers, or altering the MoA/AoA.

core_concepts.title: Class Action Suits (Section 245)
core_concepts.description:
A major addition in the 2013 Act (inspired by the Satyam Scam). 
It empowers shareholders or depositors to file a 'Class Action Suit' against the company, directors, or even *auditors/audit firms* if they claim the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to their interests. They can seek damages/compensation directly from the auditors for fraudulent statements.

important_entities.name: Independent Directors (Section 149)
important_entities.key_fact: At least 1/3rd of the Board must be independent.
important_entities.significance: To prevent corporate fraud by promoter-directors, the 2013 Act mandates that every listed public company must have at least one-third of its total number of directors as 'Independent Directors'. They must not have any material pecuniary (financial) relationship with the company.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Advanced exams often ask: 'Under the Companies Act 2013, CSR is based on the comply-or-explain principle without any penal consequences.' **FALSE**. Following the 2019 and 2020 amendments, Section 135 is now strictly mandatory. Unspent CSR money MUST be transferred to a designated state fund, and non-compliance attracts heavy monetary penalties.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Remember these exact figures: 500 Crore (Net Worth), 1000 Crore (Turnover), or 5 Crore (Net Profit). Hitting ANY ONE triggers the 2% CSR rule.

exam_strategy_tips: In UPSC Mains, when discussing Corporate Governance, you must highlight the shift from 'Majority Supremacy' (*Foss v. Harbottle*) to strict 'Minority Protection' enabled by the NCLT through **Sections 241 and 245 (Class Action Suits)** of the 2013 Act.
